slides.title: What's the Pythagorean Theorem?
slides.text: The Pythagorean theorem states that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the length of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides. In mathematical notation, a² + b² = c², where c is the length of the hypotenuse and a and b are the lengths of the legs.

slides.title: Deriving the Theorem
slides.text: Let’s verify this important theorem with a simple proof. Consider a right triangle with legs of length a and b, and hypotenuse of length c. By the Pythagorean theorem, c² = a² + b². Using (a + b)² as an expansion, we find (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Since the square of the hypotenuse is simply (a + b)², this implies c² = a² + 2ab + b², or a² + b² = c² - ab.

slides.title: Graphical Representation
slides.text: The Pythagorean theorem can also be represented graphically: the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides. In a Cartesian coordinate system, the equation of the circle with center at the origin and radius r is x² + y² = r². For a right triangle, we have two squares with sides a and b, and the hypotenuse c. This leads to the equation c² = a² + b², which is the graphic representation of the Pythagorean theorem. slides.title: Review and Practice
slides.text: Now that we've covered the Pythagorean theorem and its derivation and graphical representation, it's time to practice! Solve some example problems and test your understanding with the help of a calculator or a set of right triangles. Remember, practice makes perfect!
